The Catholic parish in Pozuelo is San Bartolomé. All baptism, burial, and marriage registers are filed under 'San Bartolomé, Pozuelo' in the Diocese of Albacete collection (1431011).

Two overlapping image-group series cover Pozuelo baptisms for 1800–1805: image group 004090928_003 (1784–1805, 90% indexed) and 004090966_007 (1800–1821, 81% indexed). Search both — they may be distinct registers or duplicate digitizations of the same register. Do not assume one exhausts the other.

One baptism volume (004090966_006, 1792–1800) has 0% recordSearchablePercent — it must be browsed image-by-image and cannot be name-searched. For events in 1799–1800, browse this volume directly in addition to running indexed searches.

Burial (defunciones) records for 1793–1826 are in image group 004090961_004 (255 images, 95% indexed) — the primary volume for a death circa 1801. Also check 004090961_003 (1720–1793, 92% indexed) for any events misplaced at a year boundary.

Baptism entries typically record three generations: child, parents (including mother's maiden name), and both sets of grandparents. Burial entries for minors name the parents — a burial record for the infant Juan would name Juan Rodríguez Martínez and Marcelina Garcia as parents.

# Locality Guide: Pozuelo, Albacete, Spain (1790–1830)

**Standard Place:** Pozuelo, Albacete, Castilla-La Mancha, Spain  
**Research period:** 1790–1830 (focus: circa 1801)  
**Parish:** San Bartolomé, Pozuelo

## Jurisdictional Context

Albacete province, in the Castilla-La Mancha autonomous community, was formally constituted in 1833 from the earlier Province of Chinchilla (created 1822). In 1801 the territory fell within the Kingdom of Castile under the Diocese of Albacete ecclesiastically. For genealogical research in the 1790–1830 period, the Catholic Church was the sole keeper of births, marriages, and deaths; **civil registration began nationally in Spain in 1871** (some municipalities from 1837), so no civil certificates exist for the target period.

## Primary Record Type: Catholic Parish Records

The Catholic Church was the primary record keeper until 1871. For Pozuelo, the relevant registers are held at the **Archivo Histórico Diocesano de Albacete** and are digitized in:

- **Spain, Diocese of Albacete, Catholic Church Records, 1504–1979** (collection [1431011](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1431011)) — index & images, 1,893,926 indexed records, 603,285 images. Browse path: Pozuelo → San Bartolomé → record type. *Marked 'incomplete' — not every volume is digitized.*
- **Spain, Catholic Church Records, 1307–2005** (collection [1784529](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784529)) — supplementary browsable images.

Baptism entries typically name the child, parents (mother's maiden name included), both sets of grandparents, and godparents — three generations in one record. **Burial records for minors name the parents**, so a burial entry for the infant Juan would directly identify Juan Rodríguez Martínez and Marcelina Garcia.

## Digitized Volumes for Pozuelo / San Bartolomé (1790–1830)

### Baptisms (Bautismos)

| Image Group | Date Range | Images | Indexed | Access |
|-------------|-----------|--------|---------|--------|

⚠️ **Two overlapping series cover 1800–1805** (004090928_003 and 004090966_007). Search both; they may be distinct registers.

### Burials / Deaths (Defunciones / Entierros)

| 004090961_003 | 1720–1793 | 305 | 92% | Name-indexed |

| 004090961_005 | 1826–1850 | 202 | 95% | Name-indexed |

### Marriages (Matrimonios)

### Confirmations

| Image Group | Date Range | Images | Indexed |
|-------------|-----------|--------|----------|
| 004090966_005 | 1824 | 89 | 0% (browse-only) |

## Supplementary Indexed Collections (Spain-wide)

- [Spain, Baptisms, 1502–1940](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1500692) (1431011) — index only, no images
- [Spain, Deaths, 1600–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1500694) — index only
- [Spain, Marriages, 1565–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1500693) — index only

## Civil Registration

**Not applicable for 1801.** Spanish civil registration began nationally in 1871; some municipalities started as early as 1837. No civil birth, death, or marriage records exist for Pozuelo in the 1790–1830 period. Source: [Albacete, Spain Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Albacete,_Spain_Genealogy).

## Language and Handwriting

Records are in Castilian Spanish; earlier entries may contain Latin phrases. Use the [Spanish Genealogical Word List](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Spanish_Genealogical_Word_List) and the [BYU Spanish Script Tutorial](https://script.byu.edu/spanish-handwriting/introduction) for reading the handwriting.

## Physical Access

**Archivo Histórico Diocesano de Albacete** — holds original parish registers.  
Excmo. Sr. Obispo de Albacete, Calle Salamanca 10, 02001 Albacete, España  
Tel: +34 967 214 478 | Fax: +34 967 522 339 | Email: obalbacete@planalfa.es

## Research Strategy for q_001

1. **Search the indexed burial volume 004090961_004 (1793–1826)** for Juan [Rodríguez] son of Juan Rodríguez Martínez and Marcelina Garcia, died circa 1801. This is the highest-priority source — 95% indexed, directly covers the target year.
2. **Search indexed baptism volumes** (004090928_003, 004090966_007, 004090605_003) for a baptism of Juan son of Juan Rodríguez/Marcelina Garcia circa 1800–1801 not already in the tree.
3. **Browse baptism volume 004090966_006** (1792–1800, 0% indexed) for any 1799–1800 baptism entry not captured by the indexed search.
4. **Cross-check with the Spain, Baptisms index** (collection 1500692) for any additional index hits.
5. If no result found, contact the Archivo Histórico Diocesano de Albacete for volumes not yet digitized.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Proof Summary: Infant Juan Rodriguez, Son of Juan Rodríguez Martínez and Marcelina Garcia, Died 1801, Pozuelo, Albacete, Spain

### Research Question

Did Juan Rodríguez Martínez and his wife Marcelina Garcia of Pozuelo, Albacete, Spain have a son named Juan who died in infancy circa 1801, in addition to the children already recorded in their family?

### Conclusion

The evidence strongly suggests — at the probable tier — that Juan Rodríguez Martínez and Marcelina Garcia did have an infant son named Juan who was buried on 17 February 1801 at the parish of San Bartolomé, Pozuelo, Albacete, Spain. This child is an additional son beyond the nine children whose baptisms have been confirmed in the parish registers of the same parish between 1799 and 1822.

### Evidence

**The Burial Record (src_001)**

The primary evidence is a burial register entry from the Diocese of Albacete Catholic Church Records, 1504–1979 (collection 1431011, image group 004090961_004, 95% indexed), accessed via FamilySearch. The full citation reads:

> "España, Diócesis de Albacete, registros parroquiales, 1504-1979," FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VTJ3-PBJ : accessed 10 September 2026), entry for Juan Rodriguez, burial 17 Feb 1801, San Bartolomé, Pozuelo, Albacete, Spain; image group 004090961_004 (parish burial register), Diocese of Albacete collection (1431011).

This record documents an infant named Juan Rodriguez buried at San Bartolomé, Pozuelo, Albacete, on 17 February 1801. The entry names his father as Juan Rodriguez and his mother as Marcelina Garcia — the same couple known from nine sibling baptism records spanning 1799 to 1822.

**Source classification:** The FamilySearch index/abstract is a *derivative* source (the indexed transcription, not a direct reading of the original register image, which is available at ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-691S-222 but was not examined). The burial event itself — the date and place of burial — constitutes *primary information* recorded by the officiating priest or parish clerk in an official capacity (assertion a_003: `information_quality: primary`, `evidence_type: direct`). The parental names (assertions a_004–a_009) carry *indeterminate* quality because the informant who reported the child's name and parentage to the clerk is not identified in the indexed record; the original register image was not examined to confirm. This distinction matters for weighing: the fact of burial on 17 February 1801 at San Bartolomé rests on official first-hand recording; the identification of the parents rests on an unspecified informant, most likely a household member attending the burial.

**Identity of the parents.** The father named in the burial record, Juan Rodriguez, is identified as Juan Rodríguez Martínez (tree person 9634-PS9) on strong qualitative grounds: the same-person assessment against the tree mob (nine sibling baptisms 1799–1822, all at San Bartolomé, Pozuelo, Albacete) matches on primary paternal surname (Rodriguez), spouse (Marcelina Garcia), parish, and period. The compound tree surname Rodriguez Martínez — reflecting the standard Spanish two-surname convention, with Martínez being Juan's maternal surname from his mother Bicenta/Vicenta Martínez — accounts for the FamilySearch algorithmic score artifact (API returned −99, recorded as 0.0); this is not a qualitative conflict but a known limitation of the algorithm with compound surnames. The mother named, Marcelina Garcia, is identified as tree person 963H-MBM with a direct FamilySearch same-person score of 0.92 (pe_010), supported by name, spouse, parish, and period matching across all ten sources.

**The Sibling Baptism Evidence (src_002–src_010)**

Nine baptism records from the same collection and parish document the following confirmed children of Juan Rodriguez and Marcelina Garcia:

| Child | Baptism Date | Source ARK |
|---|---|---|
| Juana | 6 May 1799 | ark:/61903/1:1:N3M1-BS8 |
| Antonio Josef | 21 Dec 1800 | ark:/61903/1:1:N3M1-19Q |
| Francisco Josef | 4 Dec 1801 | ark:/61903/1:1:N3M1-1JT |
| Maria | 4 Jul 1804 | ark:/61903/1:1:N39M-M1F |
| Bartholome Martin | 31 Jan 1809 | ark:/61903/1:1:N39M-S4K |
| Ana Juana | 13 Jul 1811 | ark:/61903/1:1:N39M-3P8 |
| Vicenta | 26 Oct 1815 | ark:/61903/1:1:N39M-WCH |
| Severiano | 9 Nov 1817 | ark:/61903/1:1:N39M-4DV |
| Francisca | 10 Mar 1822 | ark:/61903/1:1:N39M-Z3P |

For the full citations to each record see research sources src_002 through src_010. None of these nine baptism records names a child Juan. The burial of infant Juan on 17 February 1801 — ten weeks after Antonio Josef's baptism on 21 December 1800, and ten months before Francisco Josef's baptism on 4 December 1801 — fits naturally in the chronological sequence and is consistent with a brief life ending before or shortly after baptism. No baptism record for this infant Juan was found in either indexed baptism series for the parish, which is consistent with the child having died before baptism (unbaptized children were sometimes buried with a brief record in the burial register rather than the baptism register) or with the baptism residing in the partially unindexed volume (image group 004090966_006, 0% indexed for 1792–1800) — a null search result there is inconclusive.

**Source classification (sibling baptisms):** All nine records are derivatives (FamilySearch indexed transcriptions of original parish registers; original images available but not examined directly). The baptism event information is *primary* (officiant recorded firsthand) and the parental name information is *primary* (parents appeared in person as self-informants, assigned `informant_proximity: self` or `household_member`). The evidence type for the sibling records, as it bears on the infant Juan question, is *indirect*: these records do not name Juan, but their collective completeness corroborates that the family's other children are documented and that Juan is not among them, reinforcing that the burial record describes an additional, otherwise unrecorded child.

### Correlation and Assessment

Two independent evidentiary units support the conclusion:

1. **The burial register** (src_001) directly and positively names the infant, his parents, the parish, and the burial date — this is the primary positive finding.
2. **The nine sibling baptism records** (src_002–src_010), each created independently at distinct events with the parents as self-informants, map the complete published birth sequence and confirm that no other child named Juan appears in the family's documented record. This corroborates the burial record's identification of the infant as an *additional* child.

The two units use different record types (burial vs. baptism), were created at different times by different officiants with different informants, and belong to the same collection series — they are not fully independent in origin (both are from San Bartolomé parish) but are substantively independent in creation circumstances and informant identity.

### Why Probable Rather Than Proved

The conclusion reaches *probable* rather than *proved* for two reasons:

First, the burial record was accessed as a derivative (the FamilySearch indexed abstract), not as a direct reading of the original register image (available at ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-691S-222). The parental name assertions carry *indeterminate* information quality because the informant at burial is unidentified from the index. Examination of the original image could upgrade the informant analysis and potentially the information quality of the parental identifications.

Second, the sibling baptism records are also derivatives, and the one partially unindexed baptism volume (image group 004090966_006, 0% indexed) was not browsed image-by-image. It is possible — though not suggested by any positive evidence — that an additional baptism record for this infant exists there. The research-exhaustiveness agent determined this fallback unnecessary after the positive burial result, and the conclusion agrees; but the theoretical gap prevents the full GPS Component 1 exhaustiveness threshold for *proved*.

No conflicts exist. The chronology is internally consistent. The identification of both parents is strongly corroborated across ten records spanning more than two decades.

### Citation Limitation

All sources in this project were accessed as FamilySearch indexed abstracts (derivatives). The original parish register images are available on FamilySearch but were not examined directly. Future research confirming the parental names from the original register image (ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-691S-222) would strengthen the informant analysis and could support a *proved* conclusion.

### Conclusion Statement

The evidence strongly suggests that Juan Rodríguez Martínez and Marcelina Garcia of Pozuelo, Albacete, Spain had a son named Juan who was buried at San Bartolomé, Pozuelo, on 17 February 1801, in infancy, in addition to the nine children whose baptisms are documented in the parish registers between 1799 and 1822. This conclusion is assessed at the *probable* tier.

verdict.narrative_for_user:
# Mentor review: proof-critique on ps_001

## What you've done well
Your source classification is a highlight here. In a_003 you correctly gave the burial date/place primary information quality (the officiant recorded it firsthand, official duty), while a_004-a_009 — the parental identification within the same record — carry indeterminate quality because the informant is unknown. Many researchers would have applied one blanket rating to the whole record; you didn't, and the narrative explains why. Your hedging language also tracks the tier honestly throughout: 'strongly suggests' and 'probable' appear together, with no proved-strength claims creeping in. The tier call itself is defensible — you have strong direct evidence for the burial event and solid indirect corroboration from nine sibling baptisms, but the indeterminate informant on parentage and the unexamined original image are real, correctly-identified gaps that keep this below proved.

## What to address before moving on
There's one structural gap worth closing before this proof is considered fully buttoned up. Your narrative does real identity-resolution work: you compare the burial record's father 'Juan Rodriguez' against tree person Juan Rodríguez Martínez (9634-PS9), and you specifically address a FamilySearch same-person score anomaly (the API returned -99, which your system recorded as 0.0) — explaining it as an artifact of the compound Spanish surname convention rather than a genuine mismatch. That's a legitimate genealogical judgment call. But it lives only in prose. I checked the whole project's conflicts[] and hypotheses[] arrays and both are empty (count: 0), and ps_001's own resolved_conflict_ids is empty too. An identity comparison that reconciles an anomalous match score is exactly the kind of reasoning that needs a structural record — not because the conclusion is wrong, but because a peer reviewer (or you, in six months) shouldn't have to take the narrative's word for a comparison that was actually performed with specific supporting assertions behind it.

## Worth considering
The proof treats Juan Rodriguez + Marcelina Garcia as an obviously unique couple in the parish, which is probably true for a village this size in this period, but it's never stated as a checked assumption. A one-line note in the exhaustive-search summary confirming no other same-named couple turned up in the indexed registers would remove any doubt, especially once the identity comparison above is formalized as a hypothesis.

## What would change my mind
Add a hypotheses entry (or a conflicts entry, if you'd rather frame the score anomaly as a conflict needing resolution) documenting: the identity comparison between the burial record's father and 9634-PS9, the specific assertions supporting it (a_004, a_006, and the pe_ person-evidence linking Marcelina Garcia), and the compound-surname explanation for the -99 score. Reference that entry's id from the 'Identity of the parents' section of the narrative. That one change takes this from 'sound reasoning trusted to prose' to 'sound reasoning the audit trail can verify' — and I'd be glad to call this looks_solid once it's in place.
